source_text: claude-2 also said that the route of using the Lean elaborator would alter things and I thought *that* would create a much clearer near-instant port plan, since the lean elaborator says exactly what to do.  But agents have been getting lost in the details since then it seems to me.

fragments.text: claude-2 also said that the route of using the Lean elaborator would alter things and I thought *that* would create a much clearer near-instant port plan, since the lean elaborator says exactly what to do.
But agents have been getting lost in the details since then it seems to me.

reply_text:
㊥ ("the lean elaborator says exactly what to do") You're right, and the route was never actually taken. What got adopted was a weaker form: Lean is used as an answer key (preregistered expected output per row) and as a curriculum (claude-3's census of which elaborator features each row uses). The port still has to rebuild each elaborator step in its own Python, one 30–60 minute probe at a time, and that rebuilding is the detail the agents are lost in. The full route, where Lean elaborates and the port only translates Lean's output to Python, is ruled out by Rob's mission gates. I'd suggest first testing it on one row outside the repo; the question at the end is whether to do that.

🈖 (why the strong form wasn't taken) The mission (`M-lean-subset-python-compiler-for-generated-parser-combinators.md`) rules it out in three places. Gate 1 says "DO NOT START FROM SCRATCH". Gate 7 says the compiler consumes "the parsed Lean syntax tree". Scope Out says "No second compiler". A compiler that takes Lean's elaborated term as input would replace the port's front end, so the queue took the form those rules allow. That form tells agents what the right answer is, but not how to get there from source syntax.

㊢ (what that costs, from the queue) The census shows how much elaborator is left to rebuild:
- coercion is needed by 44 failing rows and no correct row demonstrates it yet;
- projection syntax is needed by 28 rows, also undemonstrated;
- about 20 instance classes are undemonstrated (CoeT, Inhabited, Monad, …);
- 43 rows stop inside one macro (`term[_]`).

The agents are working in census order (quotB and quot1 are the `term[_]` fix), so they aren't drifting off-plan. But each step of the elaborator takes several probes of 1,982–3,803 s each (S2b). Meanwhile Lean elaborated all 110 rows in 24 s. Side work has also taken seats: resident reload (gave a false pass), selective cache invalidation (not viable), and deriving (needs 4 layers).

🈖 (why the strong form would be a short plan) It's closer than it sounds. The port already loads Lean's native library to parse (361 s of native calls in the cold profile), and the elaborator is in that same library. codex-6 is already capturing Lean's compiler output per row (`compiled.txt`, the mono stage), but only for checking answers. That intermediate language has a handful of constructs (let, fun, join points, cases, return), so a translator from it to Python would be the "relatively small generic compiler" the mission's own Operator Direction asks for. That section also says "not gradual declaration-by-declaration convergence", which is what the current route is turning into. So the strong route fits the mission's stated aim and breaks its gates.

㭭 (a cheap test before asking Rob) One packet, outside mfuton-share so no gate is touched: take two or three rows that are failing now, translate their `compiled.txt` to Python with a small throwaway translator, and run the result against the preregistered `expected.txt`. If behaviour matches, you'd have a concrete case to put to Rob. If not, the packet shows what the intermediate language leaves out, such as runtime primitives or `extern` functions.

🈸 (one decision) Shall I dispatch that test, or would you rather take the gate question to Rob first?

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-6
previous_reply_acts.label: "could we have gotten speedups?"
previous_reply_acts.text: ㊥ ("could we have gotten speedups?") Probably yes, but less than you'd hope. A compiler written natively in Common Lisp would run its own work several times faster than the Python port, and the generated Python would cost almost nothing, since running it took 8.5 s of a 2,314 s cold probe. Language doesn't touch the larger costs, though: the Lean parsing in native code, a parse of nearly the whole repository on every cold run, and finding which elaborator step goes wrong one probe at a time. My rough guess is that a cold check would have shrunk from about 30 minutes to somewhere in the 5–15 minute range. Nothing here has measured that.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-6
previous_reply_acts.label: why the Lisp port was slow
previous_reply_acts.text: 🈖 (why the Lisp port was slow) The Lisp port didn't fail because of Lisp. It translated Python into Lisp, so it had to rebuild Python's object model on top of Lisp. Every field read went through generic string-keyed attribute lookup and generic call dispatch. bench2 (`/tmp/pyreg/lisp/bench2/README.md`) made three targeted fixes and was still 25–31x slower, with the cost spread across the whole object model rather than a few hot spots. Lisp written natively from the start would use typed structs and direct calls, and would avoid that cost. Your counterfactual is also the easier direction to translate in. Restricted Lisp (structs, functions, no metaobject tricks) maps into Python without trouble. Python mapped into Lisp has to carry descriptors, the method resolution order (MRO) and `__getattr__` along with it.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-6
previous_reply_acts.label: where a cold probe's time goes
previous_reply_acts.text: ㊢ (where a cold probe's time goes) codex's cProfile of a cold `pushSyntax` run (`/tmp/pyreg/lisp/cold1/README.md`):

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-6
previous_reply_acts.text:
| Phase | Seconds (inclusive, overlapping) | Would Lisp change it? |
|---|---:|---|
| Lean parsing + flat-syntax decode | 741 (361 of it in LeanPy's native wrapper) | Only the Python half |
| Repository-wide semantic inventory (re-parses 2,049 of 2,209 `.lean` files) | 641 | No. It's a design choice |
| Owner-index access (456,650 calls) | 649 | Partly. A disk-cache cost |
| Payload validation (50M `dataclasses.fields` calls) | 339 | Mostly gone. That's the Python object model |
| Pickle writes | 119 | Gone in an image |
| Running the generated code | 8.5 | Irrelevant |

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-6
previous_reply_acts.text: The CPU-bound Python work would speed up. The native parser and the broad inventory wouldn't.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-6
previous_reply_acts.label: the line-282 fix
previous_reply_acts.text: 🈖 (the line-282 fix) The bigger difference is the one you were after with the warm image. A Lisp project would probably never have built the on-disk object cache with compiler fingerprints, because the image itself holds that state. The resident-process idea from that passage failed because of that disk cache. `/tmp/pyreg/overnight/resident-verdict.md` found that a failed first call wrote partial results into the shared cache, so the second call started from a different state and gave a different verdict. That's a defect in the cache design, not a Python limit. Lisp has its own version of the risk: data that the old definition of a function computed stays in the image after you redefine it. Your rule that the image is for searching and a cold run is the check would still hold. It would just be cheaper to follow.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-6
previous_reply_acts.label: what wouldn't change
previous_reply_acts.text: ㊟ (what wouldn't change) The overnight fixes kept turning out to be pieces of Lean's term elaborator: expected-type propagation, instance order, implicit metavariables, erasure. Most of the time went into finding which step diverged, and each attempt cost one probe. A faster language makes each attempt cheaper but doesn't reduce the number of them. A diff of the port's elaborated terms against Lean's (S4, now with codex-23) attacks that count, and that would have been needed in either language.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-6
previous_reply_acts.label: the condition on all this
previous_reply_acts.text: ㊟ (the condition on all this) This assumes the compiler itself could have been in Lisp, with only its output in Python. If Rob's mission requires the compiler to be Python (mfuton-share is a Python codebase, and the mission has a "do not start from scratch" gate), then CL→Python would mean transpiling the whole compiler. The output would be at least as slow as hand-written Python, and the gain would be limited to iterating in the image.
